14. Versions and License

What a Version Number Promises

A release is a Git tag, v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, with a manifest.json that holds the SHA-256 of every file it carries, and a GitHub release that carries those files in one archive, brand-<version>.tar.gz, with a signed build provenance attestation. Its public surface is the names, meanings and files a consumer depends on: the semantic tokens and their custom properties, the classes of css/base.css, the exports of tokens/tokens.mjs and tokens/derive.mjs, the files' paths, the typefaces and the marks. The version number says how that surface changed (the decision).

ChangeVersion
Rename or remove a semantic token, a custom property, a class of base.css or an export of a moduleMajor
Move, rename or remove a released file, such as a logo's pathMajor
Change what a token is for, or a derivation guard so a color that passed failsMajor
Replace a typeface, or drop a font fileMajor
Redraw a markMajor
Change a value: a color step, a radius, a duration, the neutral's hueMinor, never a patch
Add a token, a file, a variant or a componentMinor
Change a primitive that no semantic token's value showsPatch
Return a value to what the guide already says; regenerate a file with the same pixels; reword the guidePatch

A value change is never a patch, because the people who must look at their screens need the minor number to tell them: nothing breaks, but screens look different, a consumer's screenshots change, and a contrast margin may narrow. The contrast gate proves no pairing fell below its floor.

Before 1.0.0 the major number stays at 0, as Semantic Versioning allows for a product still taking shape: a change the table calls major raises the minor number, and so does every value change and every addition. The changelog then describes the product as it is, not each change, and a rename needs no deprecation. Version 1.0.0 is released when the first product ships on Instrument; from then on the table binds.

How to Pin

Pin an exact version, never a range: vendor files from one release's attested archive and check them against its manifest (Applying it), or name a file by its address at a tag. No tag moves, and there is no moving v1 tag. The changelog, CHANGELOG.md, names the tokens and files each release touches.

Which License Covers What

WhatLicense
The code, the tokens, the stylesheets, the braces in brace/, NCode's icons in icons/, the derivation, the Material UI data, the syntax theme, the email template, the slide theme, the vendoring script, the guideApache License 2.0, LICENSE.txt. A brace alone is a part of the system, not a mark
The names NCode, NCode Group and NCode Identity, and the marks, every file in logo/Trademarks of NCode Group; the marks' artwork is copyright NCode Group, all rights reserved. TRADEMARKS.md says how you may use them
Instrument Sans and Martian Mono, the files in fonts/ and the copies embedded in slides/instrument.cssCopyright their authors, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, in fonts/OFL-Instrument-Sans.txt and fonts/OFL-Martian-Mono.txt
The icons in icons/ taken from Lucide, those icons/icons.json gives the source lucideCopyright Lucide Icons and Contributors under the ISC License, and those Lucide derives from Feather also copyright Cole Bemis under the MIT License, both in icons/LICENSE-Lucide.txt
The wordmark's outlines, inside the logo filesPart of the marks, as the row above says. They were drawn from Inter Display, copyright The Inter Project Authors and licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which is credited here as a courtesy: no file needs or carries the font

Other NCode repositories publish copies of the marks under their own licenses, such as NCodeGroup/project-template's brand/ folder under its MIT License from v0.82.0 on, and those copies stay under it; TRADEMARKS.md lists them.
